review:
Good lord, this is a game that makes me excited about what games are becoming.

This is a refinement of so many good ideas which inspired its predecessors. At first glance, it just looks like prettier Factorio. But it has defined itself by emphasizing gameplay elements which Factorio marginalized in order to do what Factorio is super good at: logistics. Factorio was defined by elaborate resource chains feeding intricately into complicated recipes, wrapped in a giant logistical metagame.

Rift Breaker is all about the biters. The essential resource-acquisition expansion research metagame exists similar to a Factorio map, but the game has taken the emphasis off laying belts (and later railroads) and put it on exploring the map on foot while fighting packs of monsters in action sequences clearly inspired by the best ARPGs. Fighting the monsters is insanely satisfying in a way I haven't experienced since a bone sliver build playing Diablo III. It's so smooth and satisfying. You're scouting for resource patches, but also there are sites where you can get a lump of resources, mods for your weapons, or find bosses which unlock unique research options. Slaying enough monsters of a given type also unlocks research options and it feels weirdly but satisfyingly like level ups.

And then you get the notification a horde is coming, and suddenly you're playing Dungeon Defenders in front of a wall out of They Are Billions. I've played 40 days on Hard and these packs are getting *monstrous.* I see the blob on radar and go, "wat." You fall back to your turrets and pray.

And oh man, the campaign is similar to the overworld of Anno 2205 (or a set of Terraria world saves). You ultimately get the option to teleport between a bunch of maps with different biomes, building bases on all of them and contributing to your shared pool while picking and choosing quests.

The gaming industry... has the unfortunate tendency to be slow to realize new ideas. There's not a lot of experimentation among AAA titles. Rift Breaker is really special because it's a very sophisticated version of a type of game you'd only be likely to find as a smaller project. It's a high-level realization of many concepts that have never quite been put together like this and it's fire.

There are going to be some people who say Factorio was better, or it's dumbed down or some nonsense because the emphasis Factorio placed on base logistics, Riftbreaker moved to arcade-esque ARPG goodness and tower defense. Those people think they need to prove something. Look, I love to play Zachtronics games like the other nerds but the day I say no to beer and Mario Kart I need somebody to shoot me because I'm already dead inside. Riftbreaker absolutely stands on its own by virtue of the only criteria that truly matters:

It's fantastically fun. Recommend without reservation.

The story of Riftbreaker, not the story in the game, but the story *of* the game, is a fascinating one, and one which the big development studios should take notice of.  This review is being written August 25, 2025, when the Co-Op function was added to the game, but I've been playing it since release.  I would have recommended it back then, but now I absolutely have to.

This game was made with no intention of multiplayer functionality, but because it's the perfect kind of game to play with friends, there was a huge outpouring of requests for it and the devs at EXOR set about the herculean task of adding multiplayer.  Through the long saga of this function's development, they've kept up a regular series of updates on the process, but didn't skimp on regular gameplay content releases at the same time.  EXOR is an exemplar of game development studios, willing to put in the hard work for something their community deeply desires.

As for the game itself, if you liked the factorybuilder games that came before, and the tower-defense elements that some of them had, Riftbreaker will feel like a familiar but fresh experience, with its own innovations and focuses on the genres.  The story mode is fantastic with phenomenal voice acting as well.

I cannot recommend this game enough.  Riftbreaker is what happens when devs are passionate about their project and willing to put in the hard work to see it through.  EXOR is a model that other devs should aspire to, and Riftbreaker is a helluva fun time.

This game is excellent, a fantastic blend of tower defense and base building, with a pinch of ARPG thrown in for good measure. But you already have hundreds of other reviews to let you know what this game is about, so let me tell you how good I think it is, in a very simple way.

I finished this game. And then I started a new game the minute I finished it.

Doesn't sound like much, eh ? Well... It actually is kind of a big deal. I have been gaming for 30 years or so, and there are very few games that I have actually finished. Somehow, I will play a game for a while, a few hours or tens of hours or more, but I seldom finish a game. Even exceptionnaly good games, I rarely finish. Somehow I slip out of it. Judge me not, I am weird, but that's how things are.

It takes a really exceptionnal game for me to finish it. Final Fantasy 7, back when it was new. Every Deus Ex game. A few Tomb Raider games. Skyrim. I would have finished Morrowind if I hadn't lost my save. Fallout 2. Justice Sucks. There aren't many more.

So when I tell you I did finish The Riftbreaker AND that I immediately started a new save, it  really means something. Your mileage may vary, of course.

Also, you might want to check X-Morph, another game from the same studio, a great blend of tower defense and shoot them up that served as the inspiration for The Riftbreaker's first DLC. Just so you know, I also finished that game ;)


[Edit] Apparently my review is marked as very useful for now, so I'll add a few more info for you folks to read. You might have noticed some negative reviews with only a few words about "no coop yet". So let's clarify.

I've been followig this game long before its release, and it was never intended to have coop. It was thought out as a solo game. But the community asked for coop, and the devs said they'll oblige. They never said it would be quick and easy, though, on the contrary. It's really hard to add multiplayer features afterwards.

They've been working on it for a while, providing us with information about their progress now and hen. They've streamed work in progress coop gameplay, prettyrough around the edges, but somewhat functional, and explained why it really wasn't ready yet. It's not there yet, but it's on the way.

So, the people who say they feel cheated because they were promised coop soon seem to deeply missunderstand the situation. The people who claim that we will never have coop are either liars or very missinformed.

And the people who leave negative reviews for the sole reason that coop isn't there yet as an attempt to review bomb a most excellent game, just because something really not easy to do that the devs are working on without getting paid extra for isn't fast enough for their liking... Well, I have no nice way to express what I think of those, so I'll rather say nothing. Let's just say that I strongly disapprove of that behaviour.


[2nd edit] As of march 26, over 2 years after the previous edit, the game now has coop, and the 4th DLC was released as a free update. And I'm still playing this game occasionally. Well done, devs. Well done.

This game wasn't released with co-op when it come out but devs have been working hard to make it possible. They have reached open beta stage for co-op. Never heard of another company that done so much for there fans without costing a sub or so.

I don't write reviews often, and this one I am writing looooong after I have abandoned the game (though surely will pick it up again one day).

What can I say, rarely you see such a dedication, effort and love put into a game. I mean, production value is just above any expectations from a relatively small team. It is a SOLID product, meaning when you buy this you will get:
* no experience breaking bugs
* nice visuals and sound
* solid gameplay (if you enjoy this kind of games)
* engaging progression
* continuous support (and updates!)
* ...and a lot more that I have forgotten over years, or haven even seen as I missed a couple of major updates :)

Imo not so many games can offer this for the price. Kudos to the team, you made something that I have sincerely enjoyed, every single moment of it. Keep rocking, guys!

A great combination of tower defense, factorio, supreme commander 2, and MOBA.

It scratches multiple itches from a variety of genres. Super fun! And highly recommended!

Now they need to add CO-OP!

Stop comparing this to Factorio.

Similarities:
1. Tech tree
2. You start with nothing on an alien planet
3. It's a video game

Factorio's core gameplay element is automation. You want to build a self sustaining factory that doesn't require any supervision. Where in Riftbreaker do I take a resource, turn that resource into another resource, then turn that resource into an item, which I can then combine with another item, to create another item? If you want to compare this game to anything, compare it to They Are Billions. The core gameplay mechanic to TAB is building a base to survive the waves of zombies, similar to Riftbreaker where you build a base to survive a wave of aliens.

All 3 are great games, pick them all up.

A great game made by people who actually thought and care about the user experience.

Everything is so simple to do building , upgrading , researching and because of this when you expand your base it's not a pain in a$$ and feels more like progress .

Only 3 negatives but these are more personal preference. 
1 - would like the option to zoom out a little more .
2 - sometimes the cursor is hard to see when there's 100's of enemies. 
3 - would like to see different enemies in each of the biomes .

Get the DLC rolling and take my money
I like ARPG's. I like factory sims. I like this game, because it's an insanely good casual combination of the two genres.

Neat game. Nice blend of ARPG/Tower Defense/Survival, although like most "hybrid" games it doesn't excel at any. Though it does do it better than most.  I had an absolute blast with my first playthrough and discovering the different biomes and tech. But after my campaign on hard difficulty, i found the replay value to be lacking. I wasn't the biggest fan of the survival mode, and replaying the campaign on the next difficulty didn't sound appealing because i had unlocked everything the first time. Once you've seen the biomes and tech once, the game offers very little in variety. Pretty solid 30-40hr game if you're looking for something to kill the time.
I'm not autistic enough for Factorio, but I am autistic enough to enjoy this game.

This game is not perfect. It is fun, though. The whole thing about this game is that it eliminates all the complexity of Factorio -- like... all of it. It's sort of a tower defense, except not quite. It's sort of a base-builder, except not quite.

There are 2 basic resources. 
- You don't refine them. 
- You don't combine them. 
- You don't transport them. 

You harvest "iron" and "copper", they go to your universal chests and you build turrets and power generators with the resources. That's it.

The combat is pretty fun, but it's also incredibly easy. There's a research tree, but some of it is critical path and some of it just makes you more unkillable.

Overall, this game is fine. But now I've pretty much exhausted everything it has for me and I probably won't play any more. It's not optimized, it's not well-balanced, it's not especially well thought-out. The voice acting is pretty awful.

But I had a good time.

This game is like if factorio, starcraft and a tower defence game had a kid, a very smart kid who is also a big sci-fi nerd and respects your time

If you like rts games and dota youll love this, very well made, runs well on most computers and overall fun. no need to worry about item conveyors and super mega optimized efficiency, a nice break from the culture of making you need to be a masterclass german engineer man to just play a base management game.

This is the logistics game for people who wanted less logistics and more combat in Factorio. No, you don't get to create mind meltingly complex conveyor systems to max production or train networks for resource transportation. The game approaches these in a more simple manner. Resources gathered are automatically added to a global resource pool, production is as simple as plop a mine down on some ore, boom, you're mining. Some may hate this, totally ok, as the games combat is where it fills the gaps of "what to do"

The combat is a typical ARPG isometric affair but it runs real well, enemies explode with satisfying impact lightning guns make you feel like palpatine and nuclear armaments for those times you just want them all to vanish. The games emphasis on exploration of your environment is what makes it work. From your special metal detector for finding anomalies. The various missions you get from orbital command, the researching of different alien wildlife and fauna to further produce more methods of resource gathering. The game also causes enemies to fairly frequently assault your bases from various sides based on your actions or various RNG elements. Base defense is paramount as this games also got some TD aspects as we setup towers of various flavors of destruction. 

The only negatives I have is the dialogue. The dialogue is what frames the tutorial mission and sometimes Ashley and Riggs have a good chemistry, but the tutorial dialogue that explains everything is longwinded and repeats itself to tedium. I turned the voices off to simply not listen to it. I did have to wiki a few things I missed, but I personally wasn't a huge fan of the dialogue dumps. Lastly, bases on outposts you're not currently on do not need any defense as long as you're not on the planet. You can only be attacked while Riggs is specifically on the map, this means outposts once setup don't need much interaction other than to setup a new one when a node runs dry. Perahaps add in cross map attacks? 

Overall it's a good mashup of logistics and base building with ARPG Combat that I Will continue to play.  Well worth the money.

This is a weird but very enjoyable hogwash of tower defense, arpg, and base building. Highly recommend if you don't want to think much, make big explosions, and remember Starship Troopers

This game, however, is NOTHING LIKE FACTORIO. Ignore the reviews that compare the two; there is very little focus on efficiency in this game.

Have you ever just wanted to take the mech from Dyson Sphere Simulator, give it a ton of weapons, and throw it into the Starcraft universe? That's this game. Simple industry, no bloated & headache-inducing production chains and byproduct management you'll find in Factorio or DSP, and combat simple enough that a few slaps of the keyboard should learn you the controls. Find rocks. Make power. Build guns. Shoot bullet. 
I'll leave an edit if it ever gets stale.

I bought this game because it was advertised with "multiplayer cooperative just around the corner". Two and a half years later, this feature is still nowhere to be found, and surprisingly absent from the steam store page.
Instead of working on DLCs doublind the price of the game, how about adding the feature promised in the first place?

I have to say, whoever was in the room during the "how do we make waiting for research to finish NOT boring?" meeting deserves a raise. Every similar game has the old wait for research conundrum, and the solution Riftbreaker gives is: outpost missions! So while your main base is researching, you are out doing side quests to figure out whats up with the planet and bring back more research data to start next time. This is a simple solution that gets you remaking new bases AND not being bottlenecked by research speed. It is so simple yet so effective. This alone gets this game a thumbs up. It is also genuinely fun and satisfying. Kudos to the dev team for taking factorio, simplifying it, then expanding on the premise.

multiplayer coop would've been nice... Seriously.. 

Otherwise, it's absolutely fantastic.

I'm so mixed on this game it's unreal. It looks good, has good tech behind it. Weapons and subsequently their mods are pretty cool. Damage types are a bit annoying but you're given 6 weapon slots so it's not the worst. Just means if you find a weapon you really like using, get used to switching off of it occasionally. Towers are ok, the tech tree is pretty large and researches can take 5-10 minutes even with max com hubs leveled to same tier.

What leaves me mixed is the pacing. Game is just slow. When you're trying to build you're getting constantly attacked and it feels more tedious than dangerous. Enemies are trivial provided you use good tower placement and mix damage types, the most threatening thing being all the enemies that bombard outside normal tower range making the need for lines of artillery towers necessary. Once you're done building defenses? I mean that's it. You sit around responding to attacks and the same two enemy events (nests and big creatures). There's all this equipment to make and no loadout slot that I seen. Which means you'll be manually replacing 4 things every time you need to build and upgrade, as there are things to reduce cost and speed of building.

I want to like this but I just don't want to play it. Everything is just tedious. It seems arcade like but wants to be deep. That deepness just extends the depths of the shallows. There are quality of life features needed, like drag placement(currently has draw placement), radius tools for upgrade/repair and so on but I've had this game since release and haven't seen many improvements that'd help me enjoy the game more. 

To put it shortly, it's a high quality game that lacks design needed for a consistently fun game. I'm recommending no at full price and yes on sale. You'll get a good 20 hours out of this in campaign playthrough and a few more in survival but you'd have to be a hardcore fan to want to continue. The average player count now compared to release is a mere 4ish% on steam. There is reason to that.

i do not give a CRAP what anyone says. If you like to explore, fight, shoot, set traps, drop mines, spikes, drones, NUCLEAR MINES etc every elemental gun you can think of every melee weapon you can think of and realize you are piloting a robot in third person to fight explore do what you wand AND THEN..... buld walls a base power sats radar etc.... This game has it ALL. i cound myself playing for 12 hours in a row didnt eat piss shit nothing.... THen i realized real life is a calling. THATS how much this game can grip you. Say what you want. THis game is GOOD!!!

Indie of the Year (2021) for sure. Basically this game is so good in base building and tower defense that you will be hooked at the first hour of gameplay. If you enjoy resource management and defending/upgrading your base against mobs this is a top pick. Astonishing graphics, deep tech tree and A LOT of building choices. As an Age of Empires II, Satisfactory and Bloons TD 6 lover... I'm addicted. I've ditched New World for this and I don't regret it.

If you're considering it but "it's only singleplayer", don't be afraid: devs already confirmed co-op mode for 2022! HYPE

I don't usually wait this long to write reviews for games I like this much, but it's been complicated to find bad things to say..

This game has a bit of everything I like, RTS building, Hordes of squishy things, destructible Environments and Actually useful Upgrades.

Story wise, it's simple, easy to follow, and doesn't really block my gameplay much, which I appreciate.
Enemies are your usual sets of weaker hordes with some stronger groups and special units thrown in to keep things interesting and incentivizing you to keep different weapons on your loadout to deal with them all, but it's not strict about it where it forces you to change things you like to use.
Weapons themselves work really well and they all feel useable at any point of the game. From Machineguns, to Flamethrowers and Nuclear missiles, everything has a use. Researching into better tiers makes them even more powerful and adds Mod slots to change how they affect the enemies.
Building in the game feels easy, maybe a different menu would work better since it starts getting a bit cluttered at the end, but everything that is necessary can be reached with hotkeys anyways and separated neatly into categories.
Maps are limited during the campaign (Writing this while Version 2.0 which lets you generate new maps is still in Beta) but resources don't feel scarce, the Devs thought about people like me that like to get everything they can with alternate resource gathering methods, so you won't really feel stuck during the story.
Overall it's an incredibly entertaining and relaxing game that I don't see myself stop playing soon. Looking forward to all the good stuff it will bring.

Post 2.0 Edit:
This took a while since the update adds quite a lot of new stuff to do. Original Review had me at a little over 70H, I'm writing this with 121H now.
My opinion is very much the same, great game, no bad things to say about it. 2.0 adds some very very tough challenges with the new End-Game being a logistic nightmare (In all the best ways) and the new Omega class really making me understand that no matter what I'd never be truly ready for them. There really isn't a lot of added depth to the story, it's more of an Objective driven thing, but the new Random Generation maps are awesome. Just would like maybe a bit more choice on what kind of map size I wanted.
The game really doesn't sugarcoat it with the final battle, easily the toughest fight in this game and it felt so ridiculously good to win it.

All in all, I'm quite happy with the update.

They are Billions, Factorio and Diabolo II (combatwise) had a threesome. This is their child. 
Criminally underrated game!
Good mix of tower defense, factorio, and supreme commander. Good performance too when blastin down the alien hordes. Voice acting doesn't really grab me, but didn't buy the game for it anyways,
Remember when games were just really damn fun? So do the folks at EXOR, apparently.

Great game. It was very fun.

Combat is very cool. The base building could use some different options but is a fun part of this game.

I highly recommend this game. They did a good job from start to finish.
Fantastic builder and combat survival game. If you like Factorio but want more combat then this game is for you.

The Riftbreaker is is an excellent example of a studio having a vision, executing on that vision, and then iteratively improving on that vision. I've played the game twice, once near release on Game Pass, and now more recently here on Steam. Both times I found the game difficult to put down.

[h1] The Game [/h1]

Your main goal is to build a sizable base from which to stage both your offensive and defensive actions; offensive being things like making mining outposts or taking ground to build defensive outposts, and defensive being actively defending against the enemy.

The enemy is a huge horde of various threatening wildlife brought together by the extremely dangerous ecosystem of Galatea 37. There's something like 30+ unique wildlife in the game, each with their own variations. Each creature has its own damage type strengths and weaknesses, their own way of attacking, and their own role in the attack hordes. As you progress, these enemy hordes will grow larger and will gain the aid of powerful Omega class creatures that are larger than all the others. These Omegas also have a number of modifiers that are straight out of Elite packs you might find in ARPGs like Diablo. These attacks trigger every 15 to 30 minutes in normal gameplay. They are also scripted to occur under certain circumstances.

Defense wise, you get a little bit of everything from the humble machine gun turret to giant hellfire missiles that can travel a solid 1/8 of the average map size and obliterate entire groups of enemies. Diversification is everything when it comes to building a good defense. You need to cover multiple damage types (to ensure an enemy with a certain damage resistance doesn't walk all over you) and multiple ammunition types (to ensure you don't drain your ammo reserves by shooting just one type of ammo).

Between horde attacks, you either build or explore. Building is the more fleshed out part of the game, for certain. Lots of structures, logical ways to put them together, and a very intuitive building system.

At base, exploration isn't really the main focus of the game. This has improved with the recent introduction of lootable gear with exclusive modifiers. Even still, you're mostly going to be running from one bioanomaly to another (they're loot chests, but fleshy!) hoping you get something decent. These weapons can be really good, and will significantly boost the offensive power of your mech, but you don't necessarily need them to complete the game. 

By the end of the campaign, you will need to maintain at least 4 somewhat sizable bases along with your main base. They are necessary to mine some of the other metal types, each type belonging to a unique biome.

Endgame consists of throwing all of your gathered resources into a pit to do the end game ritual. Big attack horde. Done. 

[h1] The Good [/h1]

Everything about this game is so quick and snappy. It's not a hotkey nightmare like some TDs or RTSs, and the defaults exist to give you an easy way to get to some of the most often used buildings. I don't think there's a single building that takes more than 4 button presses maximum to place, even with the variety of structures available. Combat is very similar to a classic stick shooter, with a few more buttons for special abilities.

You're never left aimless. There's always a new objective to complete. Objectives are not time-gated, so you can tackle them whenever you like, however you like. You can even ignore them for a time if you want to just build or explore.

On the factory side of things, every building has a distinct role. There's rarely more than a single way to get a resource, and everything solid goes into an ethereal bank that buildings can pull from. Liquids need to be physically routed with pipes, but that is very easy, especially since you don't have to deal with going around conveyor belts. If you're looking for a complex factory game, this isn't it. But for beginners in the genre? This might be a good entry point.

The environment is beautiful. The buildings look cool. By the end of the game, your main base will be filled with so much sci-fi crap, you'll be wondering how you even understood what you put together in the first place.

Performance is top notch. The only time I slowed down was on the VERY last attack of the extended post-game campaign, where you're dealing with the equivalent of 3-5 of your normal enemy horde attacks all at once.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

[h2] Research [/h2]

The Riftbreaker is not a complex game. Once you really know what you're doing, I imagine you could gather enough resources to finish the game in about 5 hours, maybe less, with research being the main time gating factor. And that's the kicker. Research.

Research, I think, just takes a tad bit too long. This became overwhelmingly apparent in the post-game content. I was forced to just wait to finish the final research (about 21 minutes) even though I had something like quadruple the amount of resources required to build the structure I was trying to unlock. Even during the mid-game, you'll find you need to come up with something minor to keep yourself busy while you wait for a research to unlock the thing you really need to progress. This is amplified by the extensive research trees. 100s of research nodes, each ranging from 1 minute to 20+ minutes depending upon your research setup. New player experience, this may not be that bad. It gives them time to learn more about the game, add more to their base, and explore. However, returning players may find the slog of just waiting for numbers to tick down a bit more grating. That was certainly my experience.

[h2] The Camp [/h2]

Look. I enjoy the Command and Conquer series. I grew up thinking Red Alert 3's live action cutscenes were the coolest things ever. I love a good amount of camp in my media. But man. The story, acting, and writing for this game really are not the focus. The main campaign's story is very generic. It was hard to get heavily invested in Ashley's background, especially since her voice actor does the absolute bare minimum for expressing emotion. Mr. Riggs VA does a bit better, but he's also just an AI in a mech suit. There's not much to learn about him. I can stomach listening to them, don't get me wrong. I just think the game would benefit enormously from giving the VAs for these characters actual direction. The DLC stories are a bit more interesting, focusing in on certain biomes on Galatea 37 and how they function, but really just serve as more set dressing. Still fun experiences though!

I can get behind the ultimate message of the game. Respect the world you're on. You hurt it, it will hurt you. 

[h1] Post Game Content [/h1]

The post game content update is what brought me back to the game. Was it worth it? Kinda. If you've built an extensive resource stock-pile, you'll be heavily time-gated by research progress. After all the research is done, the final building is kind of absurd. It will take you a solid hour to figure out how to pull together the resources you need for it, even with a well stocked base. Then comes powering it. I had to purify water from just about every pool in my headquarters map to get it running. There were fusion reactors everywhere. Fun? Yeah. Worth doing again? Probably not. The bonuses from the other megastructures were cool though!

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Game is fun. Give it a try. You'll know very quickly if its your cup of tea. I emphatically recommend it to everyone, if nothing but for the fact that I think EXOR deserves money for making a unique and fun experience that they've been refining for four years now.

Tower Defense and some RTS mix are both my most favorite genre in gaming. Sadly both are declining over the last decades. So this one is really refreshing and I'm already very much excited for the co-op mode next year!
Opens Riftbreaker suddenly realize 9 hours has passed.
Riftbreaker is a great game, mix of RTS, Tower Defense, Base Building, Action RPG. Decent story and graphics. Runs well on linux

The Riftbreaker is the full escalation of tower defense, to multiple base defense with an open style of creating and maintaining said bases. The story is take it or leave it, while the voice acting is decent. The script is just mostly eye rolling. 

The mechanics and style of The Riftbreaker is enjoyable and refreshing for the genre. I never had a single game crash, but the game did have a lot of errors that required moments of head scratching to figure out what to do about them. All of my problems seemed to be functions within the game, but the game itself was a worry free experience. 

I can easily recommend this game, despite the numerous times of running into a bug. Just be prepared to lose track of time. Many occasions became much like how I used to enjoy the old Civilization games.

Stompy robot with copious dakka absolutely dominates entire planet for its resources.

~10/15/25
recently finished the campaign in the long awaited coop mode, it took everything awesome about riftbreaker and doubled it. its incredibly entertaining to cut into an oncoming hoard with double the dakka, nukes and orbital lasers. galatea 37 never stood a chance. 

Exor delivered a fat juicy W after fat juicy W with riftbreaker and its easily at the top of my list of favorite games of the last 10 years.

This game promised co-op multiplayer in it's early stages (in early-access if I remember correctly). It has been several years since the full release. Multipe DLCs are out. There is merch available. I still cannot play with my friend. I have waited so long for this that I give up now.

A great game for blind people. Someone is always telling you what is happening from one minute to the next.

Seriously though, there is a lot of potential for Riftbreaker to be a good game. Unfortunately It feels like a linear tower defense that changed direction mid-development. There just isn't a whole lot going on underneath its combat system. The tech tree looks large at first but is quickly exhausted. Environments and creeps are mostly reskins. Goal progression is shallow, verging on tedium.

That said, if the Xmorph title, also by Exor, looks like your thing, do pick it up!

Until the endgame update and the mega structures, this was great. It had many options and ways you could tackle the game. You could do the DLC in any order if you're far enough, you could progress the story regardless of your skills, and get the full experience.

With the mega structures, the focus has become singular - do the DLC to get the nukes, obliterate everything. There is no more, "We must save the world and us, too." There is no more balance - it is literally, "Waste all of the resources on this mega structure and kill everything that comes to destroy it."

The mega structures take colossal amounts of resources to maintain and build. That's understandable since that's literally all they're meant for. Sure, they have some good benefits, like showing the entire map and its mining spots, or increasing farm yield, but... they're thankless and full of bugs.

Get this. I built the entire thing up and powered the final structure. Mr. Riggs told me, "Hey, the last wave is coming, better be ready." I was like like, well, ok, good, bring it on. I had good defenses, I had good items and gear, so start it up. What happened next was just pathetic.

My entire base was obliterated. My mega structures, which you can build more of on one map because nothing stops you, well, one bit the dust. More than half of my base, despite finishing all of the DLC and having upgrades everywhere, was just wiped out because multiple mega units came out and just killed everything. The mods these things have are stupid - heal all in an area, prevent damage to it unless you're in its bubble, and so forth. How is a tower supposed to kill that? This isn't that kind of game!

TLDR, devs released a massive update that reworked a load of the game into a botched mess that isn't fun or exciting anymore.

Putting a negative review on this game is kinda heartbreaking. For a long time this was one of the easiest recommendations I've been making to people. Hands down one of my favourite games of all time. I even did some speed running. However the coop updates have pretty much ruined the game imo. I played maybe 20 minutes into a new game once the update was out and haven't touched it since. Reading the dev log for the latest update that reworks movement skills (around mid October 2025) has been depressing, and a clear indication the game is going in a direction that I don't enjoy.

There are big issues and small issues. Some of the biggest issues have been how the economy was reworked. As the amount of bases you can have has increased, the amount of resources you can be harvesting at once has increased. To compensate, all researches now have a huge resource cost associated with them. Even the first ones you can do. You might be sitting afk for 10+mins waiting for resources because you don't get lots of resources outposts until the late game. Why this massive roadblock exists early is bizare and fun killing.
Tier 2 and 3 resource extractors now harvest half the amount. These changes mean that you need a higher amount of resource outposts simply to get to the level we had before. Why increase the amount of bases we can have when there is no benefit to it, and the huge downside of butchering the early game and wasting our time with setting up all these extra bases?

The resource cost to researches has other side effects. A lot of researches that unlock things that need rarer or later game resources also need said resource to research. This may not sound like an issue, after all if you don't have the resource you can't use the results of the research. However some items that require resources X are gated by researches that unlock items that use resource Y. Before you could research the item you can't use to get the item you can use. Now you can't. This forces a much more linear and fixed path through the game, rather than the more open choices we had before. You can turn down resource costs to 1% but not 0%, you can't get this choice back.

Previously, weapons and gear you crafted had some degree of randomness to them. The higher tier the weapon/item, the more random bonuses it would have. I can understand why some players would find making 20 of a weapon, choosing the best, and then dismantling the other 18 or 19 to be boring. Personally I found it a nice addition that let me have a little more choice in what I wanted from my gear. Do I want something super ammo efficient? Then build a weapon with better efficiency and throw on some ammo cost reduction mods. Weapons with different stats still exist, but they have to be gathered either from 'anomalies' in the environment, or as random drops from enemies. This is a pure downgrade, as we are now massively timegated in trying to aquire the gear we want. While the game does have some ARPG elements to the how combat works, it's not an ARPG and was never trying to be one. I don't want an ARPG. Stop moving the game into a new genre I beg.

The movement skill reworks have gone in this direction to. Rather than simple functional movement skills, they've all becoming flashy damaging abilities like in an ARPG. The teleport skill, one of my 2 most core movement skills, has been made visually and functionally frustrating going by the gifs they've shown off/the devs descriptions of how it works now.

Then there are the smaller issues, mainly visual. With coop being a new focus, the devs have decided to reduce a lot of visuals to make things more 'readable'. This makes the game less visually interesting and dynamic. Smaller, shorter lived explosions. Effects removed. All in the service of a mode I'm not even playing.

There is *one* half good thing in this update. The devs have let us keep the original version of the game via a beta branch. Unfortunately that means no more updates, being locked out of the expanded late game (might have been good? I don't know, can't stomach the early game anymore so I'll never get to play it), and the further expansions. I don't have enough time to spend modding the game's visuals back to pre-nerf, removing the resource costs, restoring the economy, etc. I won't play the old version anymore since this has left such a bad taste, and I'll be lamenting missing out on potentially good new content buried deep in the botched rework of a game that was previously amazing and never needed it.

[h1]Quick Summary [/h1]
Riftbreaker takes the base-building genre and puts you in control of a powerful mech with fun weapons and gadgets to kill swarms of enemies. Layered on top are excellent tech, engaging progression, and explosive combat. The only lacking component is the UI, which most RTS fans will have a hard time looking past. Despite the minor gripes I have, it’s a top-tier adventure, killing and expanding across the planet. 


 [quote]Follow our Curator page, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/41449676/] Summit Reviews [/url], to see more high-quality reviews regularly.[/quote]

[h1]Genre Blending [/h1]
EXOR Studios has proven again that they can mix two genres, pull it off and make it look great. It focuses on wreaking havoc with your mech coupled with basic logistics and base-building gameplay, that will ease people into the logistics genre if it’s their first, but not too simple for veterans to be bored. 

You have multiple themed locations to visit on your planet separated by loading screens. Each area varies by focusing on certain resources, weather conditions, hazards, and introducing new enemies. This forces you to mix up how you build and set up your power grid. Each new location has a specific resource to gather and they don’t get attacked when you’re not there.

[h1]Straight to Setting Up[/h1]
All major resources, used to build and craft ammo, are mined straight from the ground using the specific building for it, with no combining or complex setups, which fans of logistic games will find lacking. You do have secondary resources that are gathered mostly through plants from themed locations. You are able to plant these, once discovered at your main base, and is the only complex setup in the game with supplying water and overlapping harvesting and planting for min-maxing.

For each introduction of a new resource, of which there are around a dozen, you have to go through the same “scan the ground and dig” until an eventual change-up. Even in-game they mention this process is tedious and give you a new area or quest that expedites the process, every time around the halfway point. They mix it up in a couple of ways: like killing elite variants, blowing up nests, or scanning the natural fauna. 

[h1]Satisfyingly Streamlined[/h1]
I would consider Riftbreaker a well-streamlined game, as resources gathered anywhere are just instantly put in your stockpile. Starting with your power grid, which can be just around you, or your whole area’s base if connected up. There are multiple different types of power each with pros and cons, and most new locations encourage or require certain setups, like lava plants and gas using swamp sludge.

Ammo is managed by your usage against your production. They balance this very well by capping how many you can build at each tech advancement. Ammo is wonderfully teleported straight to your character, a godsend for how much slaughtering goes on. 

[h1]Base Building for Consoles[/h1]
It’s nice to see this style of game approachable to a wider audience, but sacrifices were made to do this. I feel it was tedious to do so much construction with a controller(I swapped away fast) with so much tabbing through so many buildings versus what a simple press with a mouse and keybindings allows. You don’t get a bounding box to mass upgrade/sell or toggle power. Each building upgrade is, weirdly, done individually. I had to spaz out and try to hit everything with the cursor. You can keybind specific buildings, but there are a lot of them, so good luck fitting and remembering them all. 

Hardcore logistics fans will miss having things like a pipette tool, ghost planning for setups, and blueprints. Although the game never gets complex enough to need them, they would be nice and prevents building massive bases with ease. Traveling back and forth from your many smaller bases is a breeze with a cheap teleporter unlocked from the start so long, tedious treks never happen.

[h1]Progression is King[/h1]
If you love tech trees and a constant drip of content, Riftbreaker will please you. You have three trees, one for the buildings and defenses, another for your weapons and gadgets, and one that gives more specific items for the campaign, along with some exotic weapons to be built. I love that you can stack research so you don’t have to go back every few minutes to start a new one. There is enough new tech to unlock that even towards the end, you still get new toys to try out. 

 [h1]Combat Feels *Chef’s Kiss*[/h1]
Combat is where the game really shines compared to its competition. Riftbreaker has the standard range of bullet, energy, and explosive weapons that you have come to expect, with some nice side variants. What prevents this game from becoming stale is that most enemies will have some immunity as well as a weakness to a type of ammo and element. This prevents spamming just one weapon or ammo type(aka can’t use all four explosive weapons at once). Along with the ammo management, it forces you to have a variety of tools to kill, and boy the tools are cool. 

They bring back the classic black hole in grenade form, four types of explosive weapons each with a pro and con, even the nuke. You got your lasers, a freeze ray, and big boy melee weapons too. You have consumable gadgets like healing, a personal turret, and mines. Early on, it will be hard to balance printing ammo vs the resource drain of using a weapon or gadget. 

With each type of weapon, you get better versions as you progress the campaign. You do get mods to augment the weapons along with your mech itself. You can get a dash that leaves a fire trail, a ground pound, or teleport for your mobility mod. You even get a mod to slow time, paired with the beautiful chaos is beautiful. Each weapon can have up to 3 mods, and there are plenty to choose from: increase spread, decrease cost, add AOE, lifesteal, and many more.

[h1]That’s A lot of Aliens[/h1]
The difficulty of this game is great until you get to the end. In the beginning, they slowly ease the alien count and variety as you get some bases built, then get smashed as a huge wave murders your hard work. Most new enemies come from each location and campaign progress made, so you never truly feel overwhelmed. 

A small sample of the types you encounter are: fast zerg-like cannon fodder, teleporting heavy-hitting snakes, stealth ninjas, or big AOE artillery strikes using creepy slugs. Getting surrounded by these enemies that counter your current setup and dying as you can’t see through all the chaos made me smile like a kid. The mix and amount of them are truly fantastic. 



[h1] Lackluster Stuff [/h1]
I would probably say a big factor in how easy the game gets, comes down to how you can spam dash and outrun all enemies with just a one-speed mod. Eventually, you can solo pretty much any horde thrown at you unless you get careless as nothing new is thrown at you in the last few hours 

The bosses or should I say lack of bosses are sad when compared to EXOR’s previous work that brought action to the tower defense genre. There, they made set piece bosses with creative move-sets and phases tailored to destroying towers. One that could easily be reskinned, was a slow-moving laser spider robot that would roam around and target your turrets, which would fit right in. 

The only boss they have is more akin to a buffed-up elite version of a similar enemy. It was never brought back in normal waves to add a nice power curve that was much needed in the end with the final wave feeling tame to what it should be.

- Without resource drain, gathering resources is a lot less important now, which is especialy noticable with tertiary resources.
- Drop only equipment is harder to get, because all the normal equipment is now in the same drop pool.
- Researching everything, so including equipment you are not going to use, hurts you now because it further dilutes the drop pool and makes it less likely to drop something you like and that before all the other RNG involved in bonus stats.

I never play RTS or tower defense games, and I only bought The Riftbreaker because it was on discount and the trailer looked fun.
I assumed that the trailer had highlight moments that wouldn't be common in actual gameplay, because that's how trailers are usually made.

Holy shit was I wrong.

I can build the base from the first seconds of the trailer in like 2 minutes, and then make like 20 of them if I want to? What do you mean?
The combat is even more spectacular and crazier than in the trailer? What the fuck???

The performance optimization of the game deserves it's own award as well.

I started the game on nearly maxed out settings on my RX 570, a budget graphics card from 2017.
No stutters, stable FPS.
I thought performance would degrade, as it usually does when you make a lot of buildings in these kind of games, but no.
I can have hundreds of machines, generators, turrets, connect them with dozens of haphazardly placed wires that I dragged across half the map, and it somehow doesn't affect the performance at all.
Mind boggling black magic.

Another important reason you should definitely buy this game is the amazing developers.
Reading their devlogs makes how much the developers love the game and their players super obvious.

Did you know that the game didn't have online co-op on launch?
It was a single player offline game.
The devs rearchitected the whole game 2 years after launch to make online play not only possible, but just as seamless as playing by yourself.

For free.

If you read the devlog for that project, you will find the amount of effort poured into it hard to comprehend.

The game is still receiving new content 4 years after launch, and they have no plans of stopping.

Also, if all of this didn't convince you, the game has modding support.
From what I gather, you can create almost any type of new content.
This including things that deeply change the basic functionality of the game, which is incredibly rare in such well polished games. Pretty much everything is open and officially supported for modding.

If you're still on the hedge, I recommend playing the demo, it's basically the tutorial of the game, and showcases the gameplay loop very well. I would pay full price for the game without a second thought after playing it for a bit.

Description: In the game you are prepping a planet for human colonization in what plays out to be something similar to both satisfactory (but much less complicated and min-max reliant) and astroneer. You end up rift jumping to different parts of the planet, exploring, gathering new resources, fending off waves of enemies, and unlocking some pretty cool turrets and weapons. 

Pros: 
-The game runs very smoothly for both me and my friend. There is some slight lag sometimes when we are both building and there have been some minor bugs here and there (mostly with the electrical grid) but not anything terribly disruptive. 
-the graphics are good, sound effects of turrets and weapons are cool. enemies get a bit repetitive by the end of the campaign but the DLC is very refreshing. 
-There is a very large tech tree with plenty of different weapons, turrets, mods and abilities that are pretty balanced so you can always change up your loadout.
-biomes are all very different and well done so things stay interesting. 
-While the game is similar to satisfactory it is much simpler and more engaging which allows for a more casual/inexperienced audience to play and complete the campaign. However there are plenty of opportunities to min-max for the sweats, especially with higher difficulties. 
-The enemies can be pretty difficult at times so it pushes you to pay attention, get better gear, build defenses and keeps things from getting boring. 
-Adding modifiers to weapons allows you to change up your loadout even more
-You can also get guns from doing tiered optional events available on every map. they give you random weapons from random tiers with unique modifiers

Cons: (this section only looks extensive because i love the game and think it would be perfect with a few improvements)
-Very annoying dialog. They just talk a lot about stuff that is not terribly interesting. events are always happening and after 30 hours of playing I am tired of hearing them. 
-Events are always happening. towards the end of your playthrough events will barely give you a moment to work on building up something you are working on before another one happens. Its kind of annoying in my opinion. I think it works well when at new sites, but i would not mind getting less events in exchange for them being much harder when at my main base. 
-Quests can be hard to follow/annoying to do. Sometimes you have to listen to the 2 minute dialog in order to know what to do next as the questline isnt always the best at pointing you in the right direction. This means turning down the annoying dialog is not an option, and even with it at normal volume it can be hard to hear when getting attacked. some of the other quests are just overly tedious, and two others have items which if broken will brick the mission; but they dont tell you when it does happen. we spent 20 minutes running around a planet before consulting reddit and deciding we had probably destroyed the item we needed. 
-Needs a UI overhaul. some of the UI is poorly designed and hard to navigate. I didnt even know there was a search option in the tech tree until i saw the achievement. some of the buildings in the build menu are a different resolution than the others (first tab). it can be hard to tell what building is what without hovering over it (annoying when you have three pages per tab)
-I wish the devs would take a break from DLC to add some quality of life improvements. looking at the mods section gives you a good idea of what is needed. I couldnt get the mods to work in multiplayer so i had to play the whole run vanilla. simple things like mass deletion, searching for a building, "building upgradable" highlight, are sorely missed late game.

This game is awesome, so fluid, runs awesome, and Co op is coming eventually.

The game is extremely fun. You have a lot to do, especially in the beginning when most of the technologies are locked. There are also many different ways to play the game. You can focus on creating huge factories or keep it simple with a few mining outposts here and there. You can optimize many of the biomes and exploit their unique resources and environmental conditions to get the most out of your production.

With the new 2.0 update, the increased outpost limit, and the infinite locations you can discover, the possibilities for huge, hyper-optimized, automated production are nearly limitless. The combat is fun thanks to the variety of weapons available. Base defense can be either super simple, using only two or three tower types, or very complex, with many different damage-type combinations. I think everyone can find something to enjoy in this game, which may seem small at first glance.

A very decent game by an indie-developer. Spent dozens of hours playing it and never got tired of it. Partially because of the mods which were previously published on nexus and now can be installed right up from the steam workshop. Fairly vigorous  mod developers have already come up with a variety of modifications that will definitely enhance your game experience. Do not hesitate exploring the whole list of them and tweak the game the way you want it to be played. Nonetheless, the vanilla version delivers just fine. The combat, base-building, textures, interaction with objects, animations won't disappoint you, trust me.   
Also want to mention their discord community where you can receive DIRECT answer from the developer if you face any problem playing the game. "Ordinary" players will also gladly help you. 
Even though the DLCs might seem some kind of lacking in new content and variability, I'm sure we should appreciate EXOR Studios's effort. The guys never stop implementing new technologies as they master them themselves, provided that they are indeed a small indie-company with low budgets. Also, there's a CO-OP being developed and is said to come up in some time for FREE. It's definitely a sign of dedication, selflessness, and faith in your own product. In the world of today these aspects are quite rare to encounter and thus very much admired. 

P.S. Do not compare this game with Factorio. They are too different and their comparison is irrelevant. Try looking at this game as base-building Alien Shooter. Ingeneering in Factorio is advanced, in The Riftbreaker it just "lies" on the background. It is fairly primitive but complex enough to make you use your brain cells. However, you aren't restrained of building a huge "megabase" with entities, pipes and storages if it is what makes your day.

Really cool concept, but it became very clear very quickly that the execution would be shallow. Unlike Factorio, there's no optimization to be done in the fields of resource flow and space management, just the maximization of production directly into a global inventory.
Which isn't a deal breaker for me, as I can enjoy romping out on expeditions with the mech suit just to enjoy some hack 'n' slash exploration... Only, portals are available from the start, cheap to build, and free to use, so there's absolutely no stakes in it. On top of that, I really didn't get the sense that my main base could ever be made "safe". It seemed I would have to be babysitting it constantly with ever-increasing aggression from the fauna. Coupled with defense of outposts, and limited resource deposits mandating constant outward expansion, the air of tedium took hold fast. When I know that all I'm working towards is new toys from a tech tree with limited novelty in their deployment, I'm probably not going to enjoy my time.

The REAL kicker for me was being incessantly proselytized to by the unlikable player-character avatar about environmentalism, and in the worst voice acting I've ever heard, no less. From the very beginning, it was constant bickering between her and the mech suit's AI, which was much more reasonably solely concerned with their survival in fighting off the waves of hyper-aggressive fauna.
When the premise of the game is extracting an alien planet's resources while blasting back hordes of zerg, I don't enjoy being passive-aggressively lectured on how what I'm doing in the video game is wrong. It's like being told by the game that I shouldn't enjoy playing the game, so why would I?

TLDR 
It's a fun little game that combines several genres pretty well, but the automation aspect lacks a lot of depth, and the omegas probably should be tweaked. Also I will add a segment on the bottom if anyone needs help with the campaign/megastructures DLC (While I wait for the research). Due to it's somewhat big flaws it has limited replay-ability but still has a decent amount of meat to it (It does have co-op which does add something). Would recommend getting it on sale.

Power:
The power part of the automation process is incredibly boring especially later on in the game where you just spam fusion generators over and over. 

Omegas: 
The smaller creatures when they get turned into an omega are fine. However; when a large creature that already has two resistances gains another two, and an incredibly large health-pool it leads to a drawn out long fight that isn't really super fun. If they do tweak this game at all I would recommend either making the unique tags for the mobs more interesting and less stat-sticky, or make more unique mobs like  the canceroth with three resistances max. 

Automation: It overall is just plop and connect with no real thought or feeling like you interact with the world. I would love some 1x1 buildings that do something so you could really optimize something. Or something to interact with parasitic vines and the cave wall so you could use loot drones to collect their drops and farm resources and biomass for example turning a not so interesting world mechanic into one that could be used for automation. Things like this would add massive replay-ability to the game. 

My thoughts on the Megastructure DLC: The only real problem I have lies in with the automation, and research time. Main Campaign Guide:
 Weapons: Generally you can use whatever you want I just recommend a few specific ones for specific things. 1. Hammer it's good for dealing with a lot of resistance heavy mods because it does explosion damage. 2. Shotgun it'll essentially get you through early-mid game if  you dual wield them and put a couple of different damage mods on them. 3. Rail gun/High Caliber mega with multiple damage types for late game omegas.

 Power: Gas is probably the most reliable thing early-mid game as it doesn't really take that much to get it going and doesn't require any input because it's self sustaining. Once you get to late you can just spam nuclear generators/ fusion and always supplement with solar/wind with batteries if the climate allows.

 Resources: Farming is the most powerful way to get resources throughout the game, and increases based on familiarity. So, what I recommend is you research the bio-scanner turret so you can place it as you run around in new biomes. As for setting up the  farms from what I understand until later in the game it's 1 planter to 3 harvesters. An easy way to set them up is just make them around geothermal generators as it reduces the amount of power required, and provides water to two farms at level 3. 

Base Defense: Don't spam turrets like a lot of guides say I recommend pods instead. For every healing tower do a pod here's the basic one I do. 1 Acid turret, 1-2 flamers depending on the biome, 2 shotgun towers, 1 telsa turret, and a plasma turret if needed. Every two or so pods put some howitzers down so you don't have to go out and kill the range creatures, and the longer range towers that cover 1/4 of a medium sized base just (like the power rod) place so you just have full coverage around your base.  so one in every corner maybe more depending on how large it is. Double layer walls, and if you have DLC use the vinewall, or energy walls and replace gates with the vinewall when you get them up to level 3. Technically it's the same amount of health but it's just a lot sturdier. I personally like energy walls because they help kill melee mobs faster.  Also I find Island bases better than one big base as it splits it more evenly just make sure they're all well defended or you'll have to rebuild them frequently because of the new omegas. Also build around terrain because unbreakable walls = good. 
 

Megastructure add on? DLC? Guide: 
1. Please don't follow this if you haven't done all of the campaign and also I would recommend holding off on the DLCs till you finish the vanilla story as the megastructures take a decent chunk of time. (It'll also probably make the vanilla final wave easier so if you want to maximize pain do them first.) 
2. Since you are most likely based in a tropical biome I would just recommend first  setting up a large water plant on the largest mud pool you can find. It'll help with the fusion generator spam and it's not really worth setting up an outpost for water the mud pool on my map netted me like 20k water. 
3. Make a outpost on a large dessert the Uranium mining outpost from the vanilla campaign will do. Make 2-3 farms for the Uranium crystals. Two cultivators with six Harvesters dispersed around them outside of their green planting bubble. Spam solar panels as the buff to them is incredibly strong, and then place down synthesizers until   you reach 200-300 carbonium/Ironium income.
4. Build a lot of storage so while you wait for research you have enough resources to immediately build the next upgrade/building  
5. Go to a tundra location put down a fusion generator next to a super coolant pool, and then put super coolant into liquid compressors, and that should be pretty much all you need. (Including your infrastructure from the campaign.)
6. oh and do the research megastructure first it speeds it up a lot.
